paragraphs.heading: A map for complex numbers
paragraphs.text: The complex plane is a flat surface on which every complex number gets its own point. Its horizontal line, called the real axis, holds the real numbers. Its vertical line, called the imaginary axis, holds the imaginary numbers. A drawing of complex numbers placed this way is called an Argand diagram, and the plane itself also goes by the Argand plane or the Gauss plane.

paragraphs.heading: Seeing arithmetic as movement
paragraphs.text: The plane lets you treat complex numbers as geometry instead of only symbols. Adding two of them works just like adding vectors. Multiplying is easier to follow in polar form, where each number is described by a size, called its modulus, and an angle, called its argument. The modulus of a product is the two moduli multiplied together, and its argument is the two arguments added. So multiplying by a number whose modulus is 1 acts as a pure rotation.

paragraphs.heading: One point, many angles
paragraphs.text: The argument is usually kept between 0 and 2π. Without that limit, a single number has many arguments: if θ is one of them, then θ + 2nπ also works for any non-zero whole number n. This happens because the complex exponential function repeats itself, with period 2πi. Lengths and angles measured on the plane stand for real numbers, and in particular the argument is a real number rather than a physical angle.

paragraphs.heading: Which way round
paragraphs.text: A large part of complex analysis is the theory of contour integration. In that setting, the direction in which you go around a closed curve matters: going round the other way multiplies the integral by −1. By convention, counterclockwise counts as the positive direction. On the unit circle, that means starting at 1, rising through i, passing −1, dropping through −i, and arriving back at 1.

paragraphs.heading: Wrapping the plane onto a sphere
paragraphs.text: It can help to picture the plane as the surface of a sphere. Take a sphere of radius 1 centred on the origin, with its equator lying on the unit circle and its north pole above the plane. A straight line from the north pole to any point of the plane meets the sphere in exactly one other point, and this pairing is called stereographic projection. The origin goes to the south pole, the inside of the unit circle fills the southern hemisphere, and the unit circle itself becomes the equator. Everything outside the unit circle fills the northern hemisphere, except the north pole.

paragraphs.heading: The point at infinity
paragraphs.text: That leaves the north pole with no partner in the plane. To complete the pairing, one extra point, called the point at infinity, is added and matched with the north pole. The plane together with this point is known as the extended complex plane. Under the projection, lines of latitude become circles centred on the origin, and lines of longitude become straight lines through the origin.

paragraphs.heading: Who drew it first
paragraphs.text: The Argand diagram is named after Jean-Robert Argand, who lived from 1768 to 1822. Yet the Norwegian–Danish land surveyor and mathematician Caspar Wessel, who lived from 1745 to 1818, described such plots before him.
